query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new predictive approach that decouples lattice and electronic heat transport using a dual‐channel computational framework will yield more accurate thermal conductivity predictions for HfNbTaTiZr compared to earlier conflated methods. The approach should capture that below 200 K the lattice (phonon) and electronic contributions are of similar magnitude, while for temperatures between 300 and 1200 K in samples with ~1 wt.% oxygen the total conductivity falls in the experimentally observed range of 10–17 W/(K m), with prediction errors around ±20% (a ~30% improvement over previous integrated estimates).
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, defect‐free HfNbTaTiZr crystals, with variants either undoped or containing a controlled ~1 wt.% oxygen level.
generation.intervention: Implement a dual‐channel predictive framework that computes lattice transport via machine‐learned, on‐the‐fly force fields (capturing anharmonicity and local lattice distortions) and separately estimates the electronic contribution using ab initio electronic structure calculations with temperature‐dependent scattering rates.
generation.conditions: Applicable for temperatures below 200 K (where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable) as well as in the 300–1200 K range; valid for single-phase, chemically homogeneous specimens with low-level (∼1 wt.%) oxygen impurities.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic-scale lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations induced by chemical disorder and oxygen impurities that independently affect phonon scattering and electronic transport.
generation.mechanism: By decoupling the two heat transport channels, the model independently simulates phonon scattering via MD-based methods enhanced by machine learning and electronic scattering via ab initio calculations, thereby avoiding oversimplified assumptions (such as using a single Debye temperature) inherent in earlier conflated models.
generation.predicted_outcome: At T < 200 K the model will show that lattice and electronic thermal conductivities are roughly equal, while for T between 300 and 1200 K (in 1 wt.% oxygen-doped samples) the total thermal conductivity will be predicted within 10–17 W/(K m) and with an overall error of about ±20%, representing a performance improvement of at least 30% over previous approaches.
generation.baseline: Earlier methods typically conflate lattice and electronic transport—using simplified Debye-type or elasticity-based estimates—which fail to capture the distinct scattering mechanisms present in HfNbTaTiZr, resulting in larger prediction errors.
generation.boundary: The approach is validated for single-phase, homogeneous crystals with controlled low oxygen doping. Its accuracy may degrade for heavily defected, multiphase specimens or for conditions (e.g., at very low temperatures below ~50 K) where additional scattering mechanisms not included in the model dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The model’s accuracy depends on the calibration of the machine‐learned force fields and the fidelity of the ab initio electronic scattering estimates. Prediction uncertainties could increase if additional scattering sources or lattice defects (beyond ~1 wt.% O) are present.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare single-phase HfNbTaTiZr samples with and without a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen content. Perform temperature-dependent thermal conductivity measurements over two regimes: below 200 K and between 300 and 1200 K. Use independent techniques to separate lattice (e.g., inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering) and electronic contributions (e.g., electrical resistivity measurements with appropriate corrections) and compare these with the dual-channel model predictions.
measurements: Separate measurements of phonon (lattice) conductivity via scattering experiments
Electronic conductivity inferred from resistivity measurements (with Wiedemann–Franz analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental separation does not show comparable lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K, or if for 300–1200 K the total conductivity deviates from the 10–17 W/(K m) range by more than ±20%, or if the predicted improvement over previous conflated methods (≈30% error reduction) is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: We have also calculated the standard deviation of the nearest-neighbor distances for several experimentally realized HEAs. Specifically, for the FCC Cantor alloy (CoCrMnFeNi), we find Σ=0.0303, and for FCC CoCrCuFeNi, Σ=0.0294 (refer to Table S2 for more details). As previously discussed, bond length disorder effectively elevates the temperature above its actual value. At room temperature, this amounts to an increase of 42% for CoCrMnFeNi and 41% for CoCrCuFeNi (details are available in Table S2). At 1,000 K, the influence of bond length disorder is more modest, effectively raising the temperature by 12% for both alloys. It is crucial to highlight that while bond length disorder significantly impacts thermodynamic properties at lower temperatures, its effect on elastic constants and melting temperatures is much less pronounced. Moreover, these impacts are generally subdued in FCC HEAs owing to their lower levels of local lattice disorder (Σ≤5%) (, ) (see Figs S18 and S23). Figure 3 shows the temperature dependence of the measured κ, and the derived values of κe and κg for NiCoFeCrMn and NiCoFeCrPd. One distinct feature of the concentrated alloys, relative to pure metals, is that in a pure metal the total thermal conductivity is dominated by κe, and κg is usually negligible. However, in concentrated alloys, κg seems to dominate at low temperatures and is comparable with κe at about room temperature. Chemical disorder appears to scatter electrons more effectively than phonons. In addition, in pure metals κ starts decreasing at a few tens of K, while in concentrated alloys κ keeps increasing up to at least 300 K (see Table 3). One major reason is that, due to the large and nearly constant resistivity of these complex alloys, κe almost linearly increases with temperature up to 300 K, which is very different from the behavior in pure metals. The theoretical description of the temperature dependence of κg for disordered alloys has been challenging. However, numerical calculations of κg in equiatomic binary alloys of NiPd and NiPt show a very similar temperature dependence to what is shown in Fig. 3: at low temperature, κg increases rapidly with temperature

Recently, a new family of crystalline metallic materials has been discovered and has come to the forefront of materials research for their exceptional mechanical properties: High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs). Obtained with casting techniques from the melt, HEAs are single-phase, equiatomic alloys with four or more elements that are evenly dispersed in an average ordered, close-packed, and simple crystalline structure, forming a random solid solution,. The strong chemical disorder within the unit cell introduces disorder at a larger lengthscale, as the periodically repeated unit cell is in fact always different due to the random atomic arrangement within it. As such, the translational invariance is disrupted, drawing these materials closer to glasses. Indeed, HEAs share with these latter the presence of a distribution in atomic sizes, masses and force-constants, usually absent or present only in a limited extent in crystalline materials. Moreover, HEAs also exhibit thermal transport properties quite similar to glasses: thermal conductivities that are much lower than in simple metals, going from some tens of W/mK down to less than 2 W/mK, and a low and almost temperature independent lattice

drafts.hypothesis: A multiscale computational method that separately calculates lattice and electronic heat transport—by combining DFT-derived phonon dispersions and defect scattering models with Boltzmann transport solutions for electronic carriers—will predict the individual thermal conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr with improved accuracy over earlier single‐estimate approaches.
drafts.material_initial_state: Single-phase HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, synthesized under conditions typical for oxygen impurity levels (approximately 1 wt.% oxygen) to mimic the studied specimen.
drafts.intervention: Implementation of a new predictive approach that integrates first-principles calculations to obtain phonon dispersions and elastic properties, combined with separate Boltzmann transport calculations for electrons.
drafts.conditions: Predictions are to be made over the temperature range of 300–1200 K (with additional low-temperature comparisons possibly below 200 K where lattice and electronic contributions can be distinguished) and for samples with low-to-moderate oxygen impurity (around 1 wt.% oxygen) with otherwise defect-free bulk microstructure.
drafts.structural_mediator: The atomic-scale phonon dispersion curves and electronic band structure, both modified subtly by the alloy’s chemical disorder and oxygen impurities.
drafts.mechanism: By independently accounting for phonon (lattice) and electron scattering—each with their own temperature-dependent behavior—the method avoids conflating the transport contributions. Compared to earlier approaches that use combined or averaged estimates (e.g., via Debye temperatures or single elasticity-based analytical conductivity estimates), this method explicitly includes the scattering mechanisms that dominate in different temperature regimes.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The approach should predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivities separately, yielding total conductivity values within approximately ±20% of experimental observations (10–17 W/(K m) in the 300–1200 K range). At low temperatures (<200 K), the model should show a dominant lattice contribution with electronic contributions becoming significant only at elevated temperatures.
drafts.baseline: Existing analytical estimates based on elastic properties and Debye temperature models that yield combined conductivity values with limited accuracy due to their conflation of lattice and electronic transport.
drafts.boundary: The predictive accuracy is expected to hold primarily in the 300–1200 K regime. Below 200 K, although the method may still separate contributions, the absolute magnitudes might become more sensitive to scattering mechanisms not fully captured by the model. Additionally, higher-than-test oxygen levels or extrinsic defects could undermine the approach's applicability.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform comparative measurements of the lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr using techniques that can decouple the two contributions such as time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) combined with electrical conductivity measurements across the 300–1200 K range, with additional measurements below 200 K. The experiment should target samples with a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen content and ideally minimal extrinsic defects.
measurements: Total thermal conductivity as a function of temperature.
Independent assessments of lattice (phonon) contribution via non-contact optical methods (e.g., TDTR).
Electronic contribution inferred from electrical conductivity (via Wiedemann-Franz relation) with separate calibration.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the new predictive approach fails to separately identify lattice and electronic contributions with an overall predictive accuracy better than ±20% relative to measured values, or if the trend in the separation (dominant lattice transport at low temperature and rising electronic contribution at high temperature) is not observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A new predictive approach that independently models lattice and electronic thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr using coupled atomistic phonon simulations and electron scattering models will yield a more accurate prediction of lattice thermal conductivity compared to previous methods that conflate both contributions.
drafts.material_initial_state: Defect-free, high-purity HfNbTaTiZr in its bulk crystalline form.
drafts.intervention: Implement a computational framework that calculates the temperature-dependent lattice (phononic) thermal conductivity using molecular dynamics and lattice dynamics informed by force constants, while separately estimating electronic contributions through electron-phonon coupling models.
drafts.conditions: The approach is applicable under controlled conditions with minimal impurity (e.g., oxygen levels) and in the temperature range from approximately 200 K to 1200 K.
drafts.structural_mediator: Temperature-dependent force constants and the resulting phonon mean free path distribution that mediates the lattice heat transport.
drafts.mechanism: The method decouples the lattice and electronic channels by explicitly modeling phonon scattering and electron-phonon interactions, thereby capturing the atomic-scale complexity that previous Debye- and DFT-based estimates did not fully address.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The lattice thermal conductivity can be predicted with a reduced error margin (approximately 30–50% improvement in accuracy) relative to earlier approaches, providing a more precise separation of the phononic component from the total conductivity.
drafts.baseline: Previous analytical and DFT-based conductivity estimates that relied on simplified representations (such as perfect bulk crystals and Debye temperatures) which conflated lattice and electronic contributions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is bounded to high-purity HfNbTaTiZr samples within the temperature range of 200–1200 K. Samples with significant defects or impurity levels (e.g., oxygen content higher than trace levels) may not yield comparable predictive accuracy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-purity, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr samples and use temperature-dependent measurements to separately determine lattice (phonon) and electronic thermal conductivities. Techniques could include time-domain thermoreflectance combined with thermal Hall measurements or other phonon-selective probes across 200–1200 K.
measurements: Direct measurement of lattice thermal conductivity via phonon-selective thermal transport techniques
Determination of electronic contributions via coupled electrical and thermal conductivity measurements
Comparison of total thermal conductivity with the sum of separately measured contributions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured lattice thermal conductivity does not show a reduction in prediction error by approximately 30–50% compared to traditional conflated approaches, or if the decoupling of lattice and electronic contributions fails (i.e., the independently measured values significantly deviate from model predictions), the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A predictive framework that explicitly decouples lattice (phonon) and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr—by using atomistic machine-learned force fields for phonons together with ab initio–derived electronic scattering parameters—will correctly capture the temperature‐dependent crossover from nearly equal lattice and electronic contributions below ~200 K to a regime where the oxygen‐contaminated specimen (1 wt.% O) exhibits a low total thermal conductivity (10–17 W/(K m)) at 300–1200 K. Moreover, its predictions will be accurate to within ±20% of experimental measurements, representing an improvement of at least 30% over earlier “conflated” models.
drafts.material_initial_state: High-purity, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr alloy (with and without 1 wt.% oxygen, the latter mimicking the experimental specimen) in its bulk, defect‐free crystalline state.
drafts.intervention: Deploy a dual-channel predictive approach that (a) calculates lattice thermal transport using on‐the‐fly machine-learned force fields calibrated against MD simulations capturing anharmonicity and local lattice distortions, and (b) computes the electronic contribution from ab initio electronic structure calculations with temperature-dependent scattering rates. The two contributions are then combined, without assuming the Debye temperature to represent both regimes.
drafts.conditions: Temperature regimes below 200 K and between 300 and 1200 K; applicability to both pristine (oxygen-free) and 1 wt.% oxygen–doped samples; perfect single crystals for calibration and lightly doped samples as in the cited experiments.
drafts.structural_mediator: Local atomic-scale lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations (further modulated by the presence of oxygen impurities), which affect phonon scattering independently from electronic scattering mechanisms.
drafts.mechanism: The model uses an effective temperature scaling derived from bond-length disorder to predict phonon lifetimes and lattice contraction while treating electronic transport via ab initio derived electron densities and scattering rates; decoupling these processes avoids the systematic errors inherent in prior approaches that used a single Debye temperature to represent both mechanisms.
drafts.predicted_outcome: At temperatures below 200 K the model will predict that lattice and electronic thermal conductivity are of comparable magnitude, while above 300 K the oxygen-doped sample’s total conductivity will fall within the experimental range of 10–17 W/(K m). The overall error relative to experimental measurements is expected to be within ±20%, showing a ~30% improvement over previous integrated methods.
drafts.baseline: Earlier approaches mostly applied averaged or conflated estimates (using a single Debye temperature or mean-field approximations) which do not capture the distinct atomic-scale scattering mechanisms; these methods typically exhibit errors larger than ±20% when compared to experiments.
drafts.boundary: The approach is limited to single-phase, chemically homogeneous alloys in polycrystalline or single-crystal form and may not directly capture effects in heavily defected or multiphase specimens beyond the 1 wt.% oxygen condition. Extreme non-equilibrium conditions or higher impurity levels may require further model adjustments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-purity HfNbTaTiZr samples with and without a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen content. Measure thermal conductivity over a broad temperature range (e.g., 50 K to 1200 K) while simultaneously employing methods (such as the Wiedemann–Franz law in conjunction with independent resistivity measurements and inelastic neutron scattering) to separately assess lattice and electronic contributions at low (<200 K) and high (>300 K) temperatures. Compare these experimental separated values with the predictions of the dual-channel model.
measurements: Separate lattice and electronic conductivity contributions (via, e.g., temperature-dependent resistivity and neutron scattering data)
Grain size and impurity distribution characterization (to ensure specimen homogeneity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If at any measured temperature range the predicted individual or total thermal conductivity values deviate from experimental values by more than ±20% or if the predicted temperature-dependent crossover in dominance of lattice versus electronic contributions is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A new predictive model that integrates machine‐learned force fields with ab initio electronic structure calculations can separately capture the lattice (phonon) and electronic contributions to thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr. This decoupling will yield predictions that agree with experimental measurements—showing comparable lattice and electronic contributions below ~200 K, and a total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K·m) from 300 to 1200 K—even when accounting for oxygen-induced scattering.
drafts.material_initial_state: Single-phase, defect‐controlled refractory high‐entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr (with controlled oxygen impurities, e.g., ~1 wt.% oxygen).
drafts.intervention: Application of a multi-scale simulation protocol that couples machine-learning–enhanced molecular dynamics (capturing local lattice distortions and oxygen-related force constant fluctuations) with DFT-based electronic structure calculations to independently compute lattice and electronic thermal conductivities.
drafts.conditions: Measurements and predictions performed over a broad temperature range (from cryogenic <200 K where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable up to 300–1200 K where total conductivity is reported), using samples with well‐controlled oxygen levels.
drafts.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and defect scattering induced by atomic size disparities and oxygen impurities that modulate force constants, thereby affecting phonon lifetimes while leaving the electronic states selectively intact.
drafts.mechanism: By invoking an effective temperature scaling that unifies thermal fluctuations with static lattice disorder, the model decouples the phonon and electron scattering mechanisms. It computes the phonon (lattice) thermal conductivity from MD simulations and the electronic part from DFT‐derived carrier properties, avoiding the oversimplification of conflating both channels as in earlier perfect‐crystal approaches.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The approach will predict that the lattice and electronic contributions are roughly equal below 200 K, with a combined thermal conductivity that falls within 10–17 W/(K·m) at higher temperatures. The prediction uncertainty is expected to be reduced by at least 20% compared to previous methods that did not decouple the channels.
drafts.baseline: Earlier methodologies based on perfect, defect‐free crystal assumptions or simplified analytical Debye-type estimates which conflate lattice and electronic heat transport and thus fail to capture the full atomic-scale complexity.
drafts.boundary: The model’s accuracy is expected to hold for samples with controlled impurity levels (around 1 wt.% oxygen) and within the temperature range of approximately 50 K to 1200 K. Deviations may occur if additional defects or uncontrolled oxide phases are present or outside this temperature window.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize high-purity HfNbTaTiZr samples with precisely controlled oxygen content (∼1 wt.%) and conduct temperature-dependent thermal conductivity measurements. Use independent experimental techniques to separately assess lattice thermal conductivity (e.g., via inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering) and electronic conductivity (via electrical resistivity and the Wiedemann-Franz relation). Compare these measurements with the separate predictions from the new model.
measurements: Total thermal conductivity from 50 K to 1200 K
Phonon (lattice) thermal conductivity via scattering experiments
Electrical resistivity for electronic thermal conductivity estimation
Temperature-dependent breakdown of lattice vs electronic contributions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the separated thermal conductivity components predicted by the model differ by more than 20% from the experimentally derived values at multiple temperatures (e.g., the equal contributions below 200 K or the 10–17 W/(K·m) total conductivity at high temperatures), or if the model fails to capture the decoupling between lattice and electronic channels (e.g., showing no significant change with controlled oxygen content), then the hypothesis will be falsified.
